findings.title: The external graph contract has no enforceable compatibility boundary
findings.description: The architecture treats understand-anything v2.8.1 as current, but the plugin is a user-scoped marketplace installation whose updates Squadron does not control. The documented `meta.json` contains only `lastAnalyzedAt`, `gitCommitHash`, and `analyzedFiles`; it carries neither a plugin version nor a graph-schema version. Consequently, the skill cannot distinguish a v2.8.1 graph from an incompatible graph produced after an upstream update. A renamed field or changed meaning of `tour[]`, `layers[]`, or node types could be interpreted as valid and produce confidently incorrect canonical planning artifacts. This needs an explicitly supported schema range, runtime validation of required field types and layer/tour node references, an explicit unsupported-schema failure, and tests using an actual upstream output fixture. Silent fallback would directly conflict with the project’s “never use silent fallback values” convention.

findings.title: The fixed concept output path can overwrite an existing approved concept
findings.description: Capability 1 always writes `project-documents/user/project-guides/000-concept.{project}.md`, but its preconditions only check for the graph. There is no rule for an existing concept, an update operation, a merge, or a refusal to overwrite. A rerun in a repository that already has a concept can therefore replace PM-provided material. The “User-Provided Concept is sacred” rule protects that section from editing; it does not prevent the containing file from being replaced wholesale. The implementation needs explicit collision semantics: refuse by default when the concept exists, compare proposed content with the existing artifact, and require an explicit update path that preserves existing user-provided text.

findings.title: The graph read discipline conflicts with the required aggregates
findings.description: The architecture says never to load the whole graph and to “grep for the needed section,” while the flow requires all file-level nodes with their summaries and complexity, every layer, the complete tour, and resolution of tour/layer `nodeIds` to nodes. Those requirements need a complete file-node index and cross-reference checks. Grepping JSON is formatting-dependent and cannot reliably perform those joins; the current design specifies no structured filter, streaming pass, or bounded intermediate representation. A deterministic `jq` or Python filter should be specified to project the graph to file nodes and resolve IDs, with malformed and dangling-reference cases failing explicitly. Otherwise the skill either violates its context constraint or loads the entire graph.

findings.title: Staleness detection misses dirty worktrees and non-linear history
findings.description: The proposed staleness test compares only `meta.json.gitCommitHash` with `HEAD`. That misses two material cases. First, a graph analyzed with uncommitted changes can have the current `HEAD` hash while already omitting or including working-tree state; later edits under the same commit are also invisible. Second, “commit distance” is undefined when the recorded hash is no longer an ancestor after a rebase, force-push, or history rewrite. The design needs explicit handling for dirty state, changed or deleted files from `analyzedFiles`, non-ancestor hashes, and repositories without commits. The warning provenance should record which comparison was performed rather than only whether the hashes differ.

findings.title: The output-location and index contracts contradict one another
findings.description: This section says 940–949 is reserved, then sanctions overflow into 950+, while “Resolved Design Decisions” says generated documents are in the 940–949 range. The same section also says both capabilities write under `user/analysis/`, although Capability 1 additionally writes a concept under `user/project-guides/`. No allocator defines how an index is selected, whether a rerun consumes another slot, or how concurrent runs avoid choosing the same index. The architecture needs one authoritative range policy and one deterministic allocation rule, including collision and reuse behavior. Otherwise the “no naming-convention change” claim is not true and generated artifacts can collide with each other or later 900-band documents.

findings.title: The optional-concept path leaves most client fields without a defined source
findings.description: Capability 2 calls the no-concept case the tested and common path, yet its field schema sources Problem, Audience, and Approach primarily from the concept. The repository’s required input, `project-documents/user/project-guides/001-initiative-plan.squadron.md`, contains an initiative list, dependencies, future work, and notes—not project-level Problem & Motivation, Target Users, or Solution Approach sections. “Degrades gracefully” does not specify which fields are omitted, rendered as unknown, or elicited through an interview, and the inputs section mentions an interview only for “purpose.” A field-by-field source/fallback matrix is needed, including the exact interview behavior and unknown representation; otherwise the common path produces a client artifact whose required core fields are unsupported by its inputs.

findings.title: Traceability and provenance are requirements without a data format
findings.description: The design requires structural claims to be attributed to the graph, requires the staleness warning to appear in “the generated document’s provenance,” and requires every client claim to trace to an input artifact. No provenance section, field, or source-reference format is defined. The client translation rules also remove initiative identifiers and other internal vocabulary, leaving no way to recover which source supported a statement. Define a retained provenance representation containing at least the graph commit and plugin/schema version for Capability 1, the source artifact and section for Capability 2, and a visible marker for unknown or interview-derived claims. Without this, “derive, never invent” is an unenforceable prompt instruction rather than an auditable property.

findings.title: Initiative-plan candidate generation is over-scoped and underspecified
findings.description: “Initiative-plan candidates” add a third planning behavior to Capability 1, but the architecture provides no clustering rule, threshold, candidate schema, output location, or traceability rule. It also sits uneasily beside the non-goal that automatic initiative-plan generation is out of scope. This scope should be cut or deferred: ship the structural comprehension analysis and interview-backed concept first, and leave initiative ideation to the normal planning phase. That removes an underspecified recommendation engine without reducing either capability’s core document transform.

findings.title: Missing-plugin remediation points to an unavailable command
findings.description: The precondition says to verify that the plugin is installed, but the specified failure response for a missing graph is to run `/understand`. For a user without the marketplace plugin, `/understand` is itself unavailable, so this is not actionable remediation. The skill needs distinct paths for “plugin absent” and “plugin present but graph missing,” including the exact marketplace installation/enablement steps for the former. The current-state statement that the plugin is installed at user scope describes this environment, not the prerequisite for every Squadron user.

findings.title: Generated artifacts have no defined lifecycle-status semantics
findings.description: The architecture lists the allowed frontmatter statuses but never maps artifact states to them. A newly generated concept that still contains explicit unknowns is not truthfully `not_started`; `complete` could imply that the concept is approved and complete; `in_progress` does not distinguish generated material from an authored canonical artifact. The overview has a similar ambiguity between “document generation complete” and “project complete.” Because the design says downstream phases consume these artifacts unchanged, the status semantics are load-bearing rather than cosmetic. Define a mapping for generated concept, structural analysis, and overview, and specify how consumers distinguish generated-but-unapproved content from an established planning artifact.
